Like the condor, the <u>prairie falcon</u> and <u>American peregrine falcon</u> once ranged over a wide band of biomes in North America. The peregrine range once included eastern United States and Canada, but is now confined to scattered breeding pairs from non-Arctic Alaska through western Canada and United States to Mexico. Neither bird was ever a dominant member of any biome.
The Arctic peregrine is a characteristic breeder in the tundra biome from Greenland to Alaska. Although numbers have diminished in recent years, distribution has not appreciably changed in historical times.

This subspecies migrates through the coniferous forest, temperate deciduous forest, and grassland biomes to Central and South America.
The northern greater prairie chicken and lesser prairie chicken were once characteristic of the grassland biome and were probably among the dominant members of their associations. Likewise, the three gray wolves—eastern timber, northern Rocky Mountain, and Mexican—were probably characteristic of their respective biomes. The red wolf, while now confined to a coastal prairie habitat in southeastern Texas and southwest Louisiana, once ranged through a large part of the temperate deciduous biome in eastern United States. While theremay be some question as to whether this wolf was a dominant member of the association, it must have been characteristic of the area it occupied.
